Project Idea:
Reticet: speech to a case record where nothing is written that was not said.

A protection officer finishes an interview in a displacement setting and has minutes to write it up before the next one. That note is what triggers a referral, or fails to. Voice tools built for meetings transcribe and summarise it confidently, including the parts they got wrong. A confident wrong summary is worse than no summary, because it gets acted on and an empty field gets checked.

Reticet takes the write-up, not the interview. No survivor is ever recorded. A field worker speaks a case note in English or French, and every populated field has to point at the exact words they said. If those words are not in the transcript, the field stays blank with the reason showing. When the worker says "names I did not get" or "I'm not certain", the system may not fill that field at all.

Built on AssemblyAI streaming speech to text. The claim is calibrated abstention.

Araxys runs a freight forwarding business end to end with AI agents on the desks. An agent answers the phone in the caller's own language, quotes from a live rate card, then hands off mid-call to a documentation agent that collects everything a commercial invoice and packing list need. Documents and invoices generate from the case file. Agents call out too, chasing partners and clearing houses. One reference threads every call, email, quote, partner and document.

It is AI-native because the loop closes: the CRM is the agents' memory and they are its front door, so the next call opens knowing the caller's language, their reference and what is still missing.

The core idea is that a voice agent is an unreliable narrator. One stated dimension never becomes a cube, no piece count means no total, and a yes on a call is not a booking until confirmed in writing. Everything reversible is automatic; everything irreversible is a decision.

Agents run the desks. Nothing ships on a guess.

Project Name: VoxNav
Problem: Visually impaired and motor-disabled users struggle with standard web interfaces built around clicks and typing. Screen readers help with reading, but true hands-free control is still missing.
Solution: VoxNav is a voice-controlled navigation assistant built on AssemblyAI. Users speak commands — "read my messages," "go to settings," "what time is it" — and the app transcribes speech in real time, matches it to an action, executes it, and responds back audibly.
How it works:
AssemblyAI's real-time transcription captures the spoken command.
An intent-matching layer maps the transcript to an action.
The app performs it and replies via text-to-speech.
Tech stack: React, AssemblyAI API, Node.js, Web Speech API.
Impact: Supports accessibility, a key but underused voice AI use case — showing how AssemblyAI can power intelligent, actionable experiences, in line with the hackathon's theme: "Turn speech into intelligent action."

Roxi AI is a real-time multi-agent meeting co-pilot that records audio of meetings to provide live strategic and technical insights. Going beyond post-meeting transcription, Roxi analyzes audio instantly using a Rust/Tauri core with OS-level loopback. A Node.js sidecar handles seamless failover of STT providers via a ring-buffer to avoid data loss.
For reduced LLM latency and cost, a Rust ChunkGraph orchestrator analyzes utterance complexity within milliseconds. Chit-chat is ignored, and parallel AI agents—such as Risk Detectors and Technical Analysts—are launched instantly only on dense topics, showing live insights. All data is locally saved in SQLite database, analyzed post-meeting using an Adaptive-RAG chatbot.
Roxi AI is built after overcoming challenging macOS audio routing and IPC framing issues. Future plans include advanced speaker diarization, proactively taking action during meetings, and full offline local LLM capabilities.
